Have you tried using the module system? Write module on the first line before your imports, and prepend public before every import
Should cut RAM usage by ~40% IIUC
Hmm. Ok. What is the module system?

Well the module system is a system that allows you to have more control over what you import from other modules and what you provide to other modules that import your module. To opt into the module system, you have to put module at the top of the file. When using the module system, there are multiple kinds of import declarations:

  • import MyModule imports MyModule privately for use in the same module. Importers of your module will not transitively import MyModule
  • public import MyModule imports MyModule publicly, i.e. every importer of your module will transitively import MyModule
  • meta import MyModule imports every declaration in MyModule for use in meta-programs
  • public meta import MyModule is the same but transitive like with regular public imports
  • import all MyModule also imports private declarations and definition bodies specifically from MyModule (not from any submodules of it)

One big part of the module system is that proofs are not imported, even with import all. Since mathlib consists largely of proofs, this saves a ton of space. Another thing to note is that when using the module system, declarations are private by default (and not imported by default) and defs from your module can't be unfolded by an importer. You have to use public explicitly to make a declaration available by an importer an @[expose] to allow an importer to unfold a specific definition in your module. However, you can also simply use public section and @[expose] public section to make all declarations that come after public / @[expose]d.

tl;dr: put module at the top of your file, put public in front of every import statement and put @[expose] public section to make Lean faster and use less RAM.

Thank you.
I put

module

public import Lean

public import Mathlib.Tactic

@[expose] public section

When I do that unfold Lean.AssocList.find? in my proofs fail. Is that related to the "Another thing to note is that when using the module system, declarations are private by default (and not imported by default) and defs from your module can't be unfolded by an importer."?

Yes, indeed. To access definition bodies of other modules that weren't explicitly exposed you can use import all as I mentioned: import all Lean.Data.AssocList is the right thing here since that's what docs#Lean.AssocList.find? is located.

Does that make a difference?
Very, it means when you run out of RAM (when the "swap" number increases) you experience a horrible slowdown, compared to SSDs which will experience "just" a huge slowdown
"swap" means that it's using your disk instead of your RAM (also known as "pagefile" on Windows)

Hmm. Why does it run the checker each time I open the project? Once the initial startup finishes after 7 min or so, it becomes much more responsive. But if I close the project and reopen it, I have to wait another 7 min.

If you close a program it closes, I don't understand what you mean. When you reopen any program it has to load everything it needs to RAM.
If by "checker" you mean why does it recheck the proofs, then it doesn't, it just loads the list of existing proofs from disk (saved in *.olean files).
I guess this is another place an SSD will greatly improve performance over an HDD, since it can read the *.olean files faster.
Does the orange bar mean it is rechecking the proofs?
Or loading them?

If the orange bar is over everything (except the imports) it means it's still loading the imports.
If the orange bar is only over half the file it means it's rechecking the proofs in that file, but that's not what the above screenshots show.
